Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open. Write $B(x,r)$ for the open Euclidean ball from [[def-metric-ball]] with distance induced by [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. A family of cells is **locally finite** here when every compact subset of $\Omega$ meets only finitely many cells. A bounded set is **Jordan measurable** when its Jordan inner and outer contents agree ([[def-jordan-inner-and-outer-content]]). A **cell particle rule** is a nonempty locally finite family of bounded Jordan-measurable cells $C_j\subseteq\Omega$ whose interiors are disjoint and whose union covers $\Omega$ up to their shared boundaries, together with nodes $x_j\in C_j$ and positive volumes $V_j=\int 1_{C_j}$. The cell volume integral is Riemann-defined and equals the Jordan content ([[def-riemann-integral-over-a-jordan-set]]). Its fill radius is $h=\sup_j\sup_{y\in C_j}|y-x_j|$, using the Euclidean norm from [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]; require $0<h<\infty$. Assume finite constants $C_V,C_L>0$ satisfy $V_j\le C_Vh^d$ and the local volume bound

$$\sum_{j:C_j\cap B(x,r)\ne\varnothing}V_j\le C_L(r+h)^d$$

for every $x\in\mathbb R^d$ and $r>0$. For continuous $g:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ with compact support contained in $\Omega$ (support as in [[def-support-and-compactly-supported-riemann-integral-in-rn]]), define $Q_hg=\sum_jV_jg(x_j)$; local finiteness makes this sum finite. At kernel width $\varepsilon$, an evaluation point is **interior** when $B(x,R\varepsilon+2h)\subset\Omega$. For periodic calculations, use the periodic extensions of the field and particle rule on $\mathbb R^d$, so no kernel support is truncated.

The cell rule is integration-compatible: for every continuous $g:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ with compact support contained in $\Omega$, only finitely many cells meet $\operatorname{supp}(g)$, every cell integral appearing below is Riemann-defined, and
$$\int_\Omega g(y)\,dy=\sum_{j:C_j\cap\operatorname{supp}(g)\ne\varnothing}\int_{C_j}g(y)\,dy.$$
This finite partition identity is part of the quadrature data.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

Let $Q=\prod_{j<m}[a_j,b_j]$ be nondegenerate. For integrable
$f,g:Q\to\mathbb R$ and scalars $\alpha,\beta$, the function
$\alpha f+\beta g$ is integrable and its integral is
$\alpha\int_Qf+\beta\int_Qg$. If $f\le g$, then
$\int_Qf\le\int_Qg$. Also $|f|$ is integrable and
$|\int_Qf|\le\int_Q|f|$. If $a_r<c<b_r$, cutting $Q$ at the coordinate
hyperplane $x_r=c$ gives two nondegenerate subrectangles; integrability on
$Q$ is equivalent to integrability on both restrictions, and their integral
values add to the integral over $Q$.

Here radial means $W(z)=w(|z|)$ for some function $w:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$, and $C_c^2$ means twice continuously differentiable with compact support. All vector norms are the Euclidean norm from [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], and $\|D^2W\|_\infty$ uses the induced operator norm. Throughout this pair, $L^\infty$ norms are suprema of Euclidean norms, and norms of multilinear derivatives are the induced operator norms. Compactly supported integrals use [[def-support-and-compactly-supported-riemann-integral-in-rn]], where $\operatorname{supp}f$ is the closure of the set on which $f$ is nonzero.

For $\varepsilon>0$ define the scaled kernel $W_\varepsilon(z)=\varepsilon^{-d}W(z/\varepsilon)$. Write $M_0=\|W\|_\infty$, $M_1=\|\nabla W\|_\infty$, $M_2=\|D^2W\|_\infty$, $m_2=\int |z|^2W(z)\,dz$, and $m_3=\int |z|^3|\nabla W(z)|\,dz$. The norm functions and moment integrands are continuous with compact support. They are bounded and Riemann integrable on a bounding Jordan box by [[thm-continuous-functions-on-compact-jordan-sets-are-integrable]], so these constants are finite.

For continuous $f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$, define the full-space smoother and its kernel-gradient operator by
$$S_\varepsilon f(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^d}f(x-z)W_\varepsilon(z)\,dz,\qquad D_\varepsilon f(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^d}f(y)\nabla W_\varepsilon(x-y)\,dy.$$
For each fixed $x$, both scalar integrands and every component of the vector integrand are continuous and compactly supported, hence Riemann integrable on a bounding Jordan box by [[thm-continuous-functions-on-compact-jordan-sets-are-integrable]]. Thus the displayed integrals exist as compactly supported Riemann integrals; the vector integral defining $D_\varepsilon f$ is taken componentwise.

All vector norms are the Euclidean norm from [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], and $\|D^2W\|_\infty$ uses the induced operator norm. Throughout this pair, $L^\infty$ norms are suprema of Euclidean norms, and norms of multilinear derivatives are the induced operator norms. Compactly supported integrals use [[def-support-and-compactly-supported-riemann-integral-in-rn]], where $\operatorname{supp}f$ is the closure of the set on which $f$ is nonzero.

For $\varepsilon>0$ define the scaled kernel $W_\varepsilon(z)=\varepsilon^{-d}W(z/\varepsilon)$. $$\dot q_i=v_i,\qquad \dot v_i=-\sum_{j=1}^Nm_j(A_i+A_j)\nabla W_\varepsilon(q_i-q_j),\qquad \dot e_i=A_i\sum_{j=1}^Nm_j(v_i-v_j)\cdot\nabla W_\varepsilon(q_i-q_j).$$

differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]],
[[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], [[def-interval]]). Let
$M \in \mathbb{R}$ with $M \ge 0$ satisfy

$$\lVert f'(t)\rVert_2 \;\le\; M \qquad \text{for every } t \in (a,b).$$

Then

$$\lVert f(b) - f(a)\rVert_2 \;\le\; M\,(b-a).$$

**No integrability of $f'$ is assumed**, so the theorem applies to every
differentiable $f$; that is why it is proved from the scalar mean value theorem
rather than from

two routes.

be **no** $\xi \in (a,b)$ with $f(b)-f(a) = f'(\xi)(b-a)$; the companion page
carries a differentiable witness on $[0,1]$. The $\xi$ produced in the proof
below depends on the fixed vector $u = f(b)-f(a)$ and is a mean value point of
the **real** function $t \mapsto \langle u, f(t)\rangle$, not of $f$.

[[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous
([[def-metric-continuity]]), $\mathbb{R}$ carrying its usual metric
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$ ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]). Then the
image $f[X]$ is bounded above and below ([[def-bounded-set]]), and it has a
maximum and a minimum ([[def-max-min]]): there are points
$x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with

$$f(x_{\min}) \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; f(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X,$$

and then $f(x_{\max}) = \sup f[X]$ and $f(x_{\min}) = \inf f[X]$
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-infimum]]).

Nonemptiness of $X$ is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for $X = \emptyset$ the
image is empty and has neither a supremum nor a maximum. No choice principle is
used.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

it has the stated value. Both are proved.

vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis

no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.

followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.

   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

Here radial means $W(z)=w(|z|)$ for some function $w:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$, and $C_c^2$ means twice continuously differentiable with compact support. All vector norms are the Euclidean norm from [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], and $\|D^2W\|_\infty$ uses the induced operator norm. Throughout this pair, $L^\infty$ norms are suprema of Euclidean norms, and norms of multilinear derivatives are the induced operator norms. Compactly supported integrals use [[def-support-and-compactly-supported-riemann-integral-in-rn]], where $\operatorname{supp}f$ is the closure of the set on which $f$ is nonzero.

For $\varepsilon>0$ define the scaled kernel $W_\varepsilon(z)=\varepsilon^{-d}W(z/\varepsilon)$. $$S_\varepsilon f(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^d}f(x-z)W_\varepsilon(z)\,dz,\qquad D_\varepsilon f(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^d}f(y)\nabla W_\varepsilon(x-y)\,dy.$$
For each fixed $x$, both scalar integrands and every component of the vector integrand are continuous and compactly supported, hence Riemann integrable on a bounding Jordan box by [[thm-continuous-functions-on-compact-jordan-sets-are-integrable]]. A bounded set is **Jordan measurable** when its Jordan inner and outer contents agree ([[def-jordan-inner-and-outer-content]]). A **cell particle rule** is a nonempty locally finite family of bounded Jordan-measurable cells $C_j\subseteq\Omega$ whose interiors are disjoint and whose union covers $\Omega$ up to their shared boundaries, together with nodes $x_j\in C_j$ and positive volumes $V_j=\int 1_{C_j}$. $$\rho_i(q)=\sum_{j=1}^Nm_jW_\varepsilon(q_i-q_j),\qquad p_i=P(\rho_i,e_i),\qquad A_i=\frac{p_i}{\rho_i^2}.$$

The state domain is U={ (q,v,e): ρ_i(q)>0 for every i }. On U, the fixed-width semidiscrete system is

$$\dot q_i=v_i,\qquad \dot v_i=-\sum_{j=1}^Nm_j(A_i+A_j)\nabla W_\varepsilon(q_i-q_j),\qquad \dot e_i=A_i\sum_{j=1}^Nm_j(v_i-v_j)\cdot\nabla W_\varepsilon(q_i-q_j).$$

It has fixed masses and fixed ε, includes the displayed matched internal-energy equation, and contains no artificial viscosity. No continuum Euler convergence is part of this definition.

The cell volume integral is Riemann-defined and equals the Jordan content ([[def-riemann-integral-over-a-jordan-set]]). Its fill radius is $h=\sup_j\sup_{y\in C_j}|y-x_j|$, using the Euclidean norm from [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]; require $0<h<\infty$. Assume finite constants $C_V,C_L>0$ satisfy $V_j\le C_Vh^d$ and the local volume bound

$$\sum_{j:C_j\cap B(x,r)\ne\varnothing}V_j\le C_L(r+h)^d$$

for every $x\in\mathbb R^d$ and $r>0$. For continuous $g:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ with compact support contained in $\Omega$ (support as in [[def-support-and-compactly-supported-riemann-integral-in-rn]]), define $Q_hg=\sum_jV_jg(x_j)$; local finiteness makes this sum finite. At kernel width $\varepsilon$, an evaluation point is **interior** when $B(x,R\varepsilon+2h)\subset\Omega$. For periodic calculations, use the periodic extensions of the field and particle rule on $\mathbb R^d$, so no kernel support is truncated.

The cell rule is integration-compatible: for every continuous $g:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ with compact support contained in $\Omega$, only finitely many cells meet $\operatorname{supp}(g)$, every cell integral appearing below is Riemann-defined, and
$$\int_\Omega g(y)\,dy=\sum_{j:C_j\cap\operatorname{supp}(g)\ne\varnothing}\int_{C_j}g(y)\,dy.$$
This finite partition identity is part of the quadrature data.

Let f∈C³(R^d) have bounded third derivative and define D_εf(x)=∫f(y)∇W_ε(x−y)dy. Then for every ε>0 and x∈R^d,

$$|D_\varepsilon f(x)-\nabla f(x)|\le \frac{m_3}{6}\varepsilon^2\|D^3f\|_\infty,$$

where ||D³f||∞ is the supremum of the operator norm of the trilinear derivative.
Every continuous real function on a compact Jordan measurable set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is Riemann integrable over $E$.

Let $a < c < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be bounded
([[def-bounded-set]]). Then:

1. $f$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]) **if and only if** its
   restrictions to $[a,c]$ and to $[c,b]$ are integrable;
2. and in that case
   $$\int_a^b f \;=\; \int_a^c f \;+\; \int_c^b f .$$
3. **Oriented form.** Let $\alpha < \beta$ be reals, let $f : [\alpha,\beta] \to
   \mathbb{R}$ be integrable, and let $u, v, w \in [\alpha,\beta]$ be arbitrary.
   Then, with the convention of [[def-oriented-integral]],
   $$\int_u^v f \;+\; \int_v^w f \;=\; \int_u^w f .$$

Claim 3 is where [[def-oriented-integral]] earns its place: it holds for every
arrangement of the three points, including the degenerate ones, and it is the
form used everywhere below.

Positions q_i and velocities v_i lie in R^d with the Euclidean inner product from [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], and specific internal energies e_i lie in R. Define

$$\rho_i(q)=\sum_{j=1}^Nm_jW_\varepsilon(q_i-q_j),\qquad p_i=P(\rho_i,e_i),\qquad A_i=\frac{p_i}{\rho_i^2}.$$

The state domain is U={ (q,v,e): ρ_i(q)>0 for every i }. On U, the fixed-width semidiscrete system is

$$\dot q_i=v_i,\qquad \dot v_i=-\sum_{j=1}^Nm_j(A_i+A_j)\nabla W_\varepsilon(q_i-q_j),\qquad \dot e_i=A_i\sum_{j=1}^Nm_j(v_i-v_j)\cdot\nabla W_\varepsilon(q_i-q_j).$$

A controlled tube is a compact subset of U on which ρ_i≥ρ_*>0 for every i. The system is semidiscrete: time remains continuous while the spatial state is represented by finitely many particles.
